title: Structures, Unions, Enums & Bit-fields
relevance: C composite types, padding/alignment, unions, and bit packing are staples of systems SDE interviews and OAs that probe whether candidates understand real memory layout beyond language syntax.

phases.goal: Establish what structs, unions, enums, and bit-fields are and how they are declared and accessed.

must_hit.point: A structure is a contiguous block of memory containing a sequence of named members of potentially different types.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines a struct as grouped heterogeneous members sharing one namespace in sequential storage.

must_hit.point: A struct tag alone requires the struct keyword on every declaration; a typedef alias lets you omit it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They contrast struct Point p1 with typedef struct { ... } Point; Point p2.

must_hit.point: Members are accessed with ., and C99 designated initializers map values by name; unspecified designated members are zero-initialized.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They prefer { .y = 20, .x = 10 } over brittle positional init and note omitted fields become zero.

must_hit.point: A union allocates exactly enough memory for its largest member; all members start at the same address (offset 0) and writing one overwrites the others.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They explain overlapping storage like a shared safe, not side-by-side layout.

must_hit.point: Enums assign names to integer constants; by default the first is 0 and later ones increment by 1, and in C those constants leak into the surrounding scope.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They mention default numbering and why names are prefixed (e.g. STATE_IDLE) to avoid collisions.

must_hit.point: Bit-fields let you specify the exact number of bits a member occupies within an integer word.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They describe packing multiple narrow fields into one word for registers or dense packing.

probes: What is the difference between a struct and a union in how members occupy memory?
Why do C programmers usually prefix enum constants like STATE_IDLE?

hints.1: Think about whether members sit next to each other or share one region.
hints.2: Struct = sequential contiguous members; union = same address, size of largest; enums are named ints that enter the enclosing scope.
hints.3: Say: struct Point { int x,y; }; needs struct or a typedef; union Data { uint32_t raw; float f; char str[4]; } overlaps at offset 0; enums default from 0 unless set explicitly.

phases.goal: Explain alignment/padding, reordering, packed layouts, pointers/arrow, self-reference, type punning, FAMs, and offsetof.

must_hit.point: sizeof(struct bad_layout) with char, int, char is typically 12 bytes, not 6, because the compiler injects padding so int is aligned and trailing padding keeps array elements aligned.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They walk through padding after the first char and trailing padding so overall size is a multiple of the max member alignment.

must_hit.point: A structure's overall alignment is the largest alignment of any member, and its total size must be a multiple of that alignment; _Alignof queries alignment (C11).
must_hit.evidence_hint: They state the absolute alignment/size rule rather than only giving an example number.

must_hit.point: Reordering members largest-alignment-first yields sizeof(struct good_layout) of 8 bytes; a traced 64-bit layout shrinks from 24 bytes to 16 bytes when reordered.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They reorder int before chars, or pointer/int/char, and cite the smaller sizeof.

must_hit.point: __attribute__((packed)) (or #pragma pack) can force a network_header of char plus int to exactly 5 bytes with no padding.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They name a packed attribute/pragma and state the resulting exact size.

must_hit.point: Pass structs by pointer (const if read-only); ptr->member is sugar for (*ptr).member; a struct may contain a pointer to its own type but not an instance of itself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They cite copy cost, arrow syntax, and fixed-size pointers enabling lists/trees.

must_hit.point: In C, reading a different union member than last written is defined type punning of the object representation; a Flexible Array Member must be last, and sizeof excludes that array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They contrast C union punning with needing a tag for safety, and malloc(sizeof(Vector) + N * sizeof(element)) for FAMs.

must_hit.point: offsetof(type, member) from stddef.h gives a member's byte offset at compile time without creating an instance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They name offsetof and describe the null-pointer-to-struct compile-time trick.

probes: Why is sizeof(struct { char a; int b; char c; }) typically larger than the sum of the member sizes?
How do you get a member's offset in a struct without allocating one?

hints.1: Ask what the CPU needs for an int's address, and what happens between array elements.
hints.2: Alignment forces padding after char before int; trailing padding makes size a multiple of max alignment; offsetof is the compile-time answer.
hints.3: Expect ~12 for bad_layout, 8 after reordering chars together; packed network_header is 5; Trace 24→16 on 64-bit; use offsetof from stddef.h.

phases.goal: Weigh packing, passing style, and bit-field portability against correctness and speed.

must_hit.point: Packed structs save memory/match wire layouts but can incur severe performance cost where unaligned loads need byte-by-byte access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They pair memory/ABI wins with slower generated code on architectures without cheap unaligned loads.

must_hit.point: Passing a large struct by value copies every byte; passing a pointer avoids that overhead (const when mutation is not needed).
must_hit.evidence_hint: They recommend pointer parameters for large structs and mention const for read-only APIs.

must_hit.point: Bit-fields pack tightly for registers, but ordering is implementation-defined, so portable exact hardware maps should use bitwise operations instead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They refuse to rely on bit-field layout across compilers/ABIs and prefer masks/shifts for portable register maps.

must_hit.point: Returning a struct by value may be optimized with RVO, but an out-pointer remains a common explicit C idiom.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They acknowledge RVO yet still describe writing through a caller-provided pointer as idiomatic C.

probes: When would you pack a struct, and what do you give up?
Would you model a hardware register with bit-fields or with masks—and why?

hints.1: Separate space/layout needs from speed and portability.
hints.2: Packed/wire/HW vs unaligned cost; by-value copy vs pointer; bit-field order is not portable.
hints.3: Say: pack for packets/HW size match but expect slow unaligned access; pass large structs by pointer; use bitwise ops when register bit order must be portable.

phases.goal: Apply composite types to variants, trees/lists, and safe dynamic data handling.

must_hit.point: Self-referential nodes use a pointer to the same struct type (e.g. next or left/right) as the basis of linked lists and trees; the typedef alias cannot be used inside the incomplete definition.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They write struct Node { ... struct Node *next; } or TreeNode left/right pointers using the tag.

must_hit.point: A tagged union pairs an enum tag with a union (often anonymous) so code knows which member is active before reading it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They show DataType/ValType plus union { int i; float f; } and a switch on the tag.

must_hit.point: Since C11, anonymous nested struct/union members project into the enclosing scope (e.g. Player.x without an intermediate name).
must_hit.evidence_hint: They access nested fields as if declared on the outer struct when the inner type is unnamed.

must_hit.point: Allocate a FAM struct with malloc(sizeof(Vector) + 100 * sizeof(int)) so capacity lives in the header and data[] trails it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They place the incomplete array last and size the allocation as header plus element storage.

probes: How would you represent a value that is either an int or a float safely in C?
Complete a binary tree node that needs left and right child pointers.

hints.1: You need both the payload storage and a way to know which kind is live.
hints.2: Enum tag + union members; tree children are pointers to struct TreeNode, not embedded nodes.
hints.3: typedef struct { ValType type; union { int i; float f; }; } Value; and struct TreeNode *right; beside *left.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Packing (__attribute__((packed)) / #pragma pack) removes padding for HW/network layouts (e.g. exact 5-byte header) but can force slow byte-wise access on platforms that fault or penalize unaligned loads; default layout favors speed and alignment.

tradeoffs.topic: Pass struct by value vs by pointer
tradeoffs.strong_answer: By-value copies the whole object and is costly for large structs; pass a pointer (const if read-only) to avoid the copy. Return-by-value may use RVO, but out-pointers stay a clear C idiom.

tradeoffs.topic: Bit-fields vs bitwise masks for hardware registers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Bit-fields express width compactly in one word, but member order is implementation-defined (e.g. LSB-vs-MSB packing), so portable exact register maps should use explicit bitwise operations instead.
Positional initializers break when member order changes; C99 designated initializers bind by name and zero any unspecified members, making init robust to reordering.

gotchas.trap: Treating a struct as a raw byte blob for disk or network I/O
gotchas.correction: Padding holds garbage and layout varies by compiler/architecture; serialize field-by-field or use an explicitly packed, agreed wire format.

gotchas.trap: Assuming C++ union type punning works like C
gotchas.correction: In C, reading a different union member than last written is defined as reading the overlapping object representation; in C++ reading an inactive member is undefined behavior.

gotchas.trap: Relying on bit-field member order for portable register maps
gotchas.correction: Ordering is implementation-defined; prefer masks and shifts when exact bit positions must be portable.

gotchas.trap: Expecting sizeof(struct) to equal the sum of member sizes
gotchas.correction: The compiler inserts padding for alignment and trailing padding so size is a multiple of the struct's overall alignment (max member alignment).

gotchas.trap: Embedding a struct instance of the same type inside itself
gotchas.correction: That would make size infinite; only a pointer to the same type is allowed, and you must use the struct tag because a typedef alias is incomplete until the closing brace.

gotchas.trap: Defining the same unprefixed enumerator name in two enums in one scope
gotchas.correction: C enum constants leak into the surrounding scope, so use prefixed names like STATE_IDLE.
